summary: This informational RFC registers the text/markdown media type, so that files in Markdown, a family of plain-text formatting syntaxes that can be converted to HTML and other markup, can be labeled correctly when sent over the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: Markdown is a simple way to write bold and headings with plain symbols. This gives it an official label so computers know what kind of file it is.

questions: what is the mime type for markdown
what is the text/markdown media type
subtitle: The official Internet media type for plain-text formatted documents

tldr.problem: Markdown files sent over the Internet need an official label so systems know they are Markdown and not plain text, while different Markdown variants need a way to signal their specific syntax flavors.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers text/markdown as a MIME media type with a required charset parameter and an optional variant parameter to identify which Markdown flavor the document uses.
tldr.outcome: Markdown content can now be properly identified in Internet protocols, and tools can understand which variant syntax to expect, enabling better interoperability.

today: RFC 7763 is an Informational RFC published in March 2016 and remains the official IANA registration for the text/markdown media type. The variant registry it establishes continues to accept new registrations. RFC 7764 provides additional guidance and registers several common Markdown variants.

sections.title: What Is Markdown
sections.content: Markdown is a family of plain-text formatting syntaxes that can be converted to HTML and other markup languages. Unlike formal markup languages such as XML or HTML, which have strict syntax rules, Markdown uses simple symbols—asterisks for emphasis, hash marks for headings, brackets for links—that look like what they represent. Markdown was created in 2004 by John Gruber and has become widely adopted by web applications and online services. The paradigmatic use case is the Markdown editor: an application that shows the plain Markdown on one side and the rendered output (usually HTML) on the other, allowing users to write and preview in real time.
sections.plainLanguage: Markdown lets you write text with simple symbols: `*bold*` makes bold, `#` makes headings, and `[link text](url)` makes links. It looks like what it means, so it is easy to learn.

sections.title: The Philosophy: Simple, Forgiving, Widely Used
sections.content: Markdown's design philosophy emphasizes ease of use over strict rules. There is no such thing as invalid Markdown; the syntax is flexible and forgiving. Unlike XML, which rejects any document that does not follow strict rules exactly, Markdown processors do their best to make sense of the input. This informal, human-friendly approach is what makes Markdown accessible to non-technical users. Since its creation, Markdown has become an Internet meme, adapted by different communities for their specific needs: scholars use it for academic writing, screenwriters adapted it for scripts, and mathematicians created extensions for formulas. All these variants share the core elements of Markdown while extending it for their purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: Markdown does not have strict rules like XML. If something looks close to the syntax, Markdown tries to understand it anyway. This makes it easy for anyone to use, even without special training.

sections.title: Registering text/markdown
sections.content: This RFC registers text/markdown as an official IANA media type. The registration specifies two parameters: charset (required) indicates the text encoding, such as UTF-8; variant (optional) identifies which Markdown variant the document uses, such as Original, GitHub-Flavored, or Pandoc. When the variant parameter is omitted, the interpretation is entirely up to the receiver. The charset parameter must be explicit because many Markdown processors work with plain US-ASCII characters and do not apply default encoding. The media type label allows Markdown content to be properly identified in email, HTTP, and other Internet protocols, while still remaining plain text.
sections.plainLanguage: The media type is `text/markdown` with two settings: the charset (like UTF-8) and optional variant (which flavor of Markdown). This tells computers it is Markdown and helps them understand it correctly.

sections.title: Variants and Fragment Identifiers
sections.content: Because Markdown has evolved into many different flavors, the RFC establishes a variant registry managed by IANA. Anyone can register a variant by providing documentation and contact information on a First Come, First Served basis. The registration includes the variant identifier, name, description, references, and contact details. The RFC defines fragment identifiers for addressing specific parts of Markdown documents, such as a specific line using the syntax `#line=10`. Variants are free to define additional parameters and fragment identifier syntaxes suited to their specific use cases. The variant names Standard, Common, and Markdown are reserved and cannot be registered to avoid confusion with the generic text/markdown registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Different communities can register their own Markdown flavors with IANA, so GitHub Markdown, Pandoc, and others have official variant names. Fragment identifiers let you link to specific parts of a document, like `#line=10` for the tenth line.

sections.title: How Markdown Becomes Interoperable
sections.content: Markdown variations are designed to be human-readable across platforms but not necessarily compatible with each other. Syntax in one Markdown variant may be interpreted differently in another, leading to degraded output. The variant parameter helps: senders should avoid variants that intended recipients do not understand, and receivers should only accept variants they explicitly recognize. When Markdown is processed in advance into a target format like HTML, ambiguities are eliminated, but the conversion may not be reversible. Markdown content also needs to carry its variant metadata when it moves to storage systems like databases or file systems where media types are not available; the RFC discusses strategies such as including the variant in the filename or storing it in file attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Markdown flavors look similar but might work differently. The variant label helps receivers know what syntax to expect. When Markdown moves to files or databases, the variant can be saved in the filename or in special file properties.

sections.title: Desired Output Format
sections.content: The RFC defines an optional Content-Disposition parameter called preview-type that indicates the desired output format when Markdown is processed. For example, an author might set preview-type to text/html or application/pdf to signal which output they want. This primarily affects the right-hand side of a split-screen Markdown editor. The reflexive value text/markdown means the author does not want Markdown processing at all; the receiver should present the source as-is. Implementations should support HTML and XHTML output, as these are suitable for most purposes, but Markdown increasingly targets other formats like TeX, PDF, OPML, and e-books.
sections.plainLanguage: The preview-type setting tells Markdown processors what kind of output to make: HTML, PDF, or even just plain Markdown. This helps tools show the result you want.
